title: How the queen moves
summary: The queen combines rook and bishop: lines and diagonals, any distance.

steps.md: The **queen** moves like a rook *and* a bishop: along ranks, files and diagonals, any distance, no jumping. It is the strongest piece (about 9 pawns), but it cannot move like a knight.
A queen on d4 radiates in eight directions and controls 27 squares on an empty board.

steps.prompt: Move the queen diagonally to a7.

steps.explain: Like a rook, along the 4th rank.

steps.prompt: Reach h7 in a single move.
steps.explain: The diagonal d3-e4-f5-g6-h7. Long diagonal moves are easy to overlook, so scan all eight directions.

steps.question: Can the queen jump from d1 to f2 in one move (a knight-shaped jump)?
choices: No, the queen has no knight move
Only at the start of the game
steps.explain: The queen does everything rooks and bishops do, nothing more. The knight's L-jump is unique to the knight.

steps.question: Why is it risky to bring the queen out very early?
choices: Enemy pieces can attack it and develop at the same time
It is against the rules before move 5
steps.explain: Because the queen is worth so much, it must run whenever it is attacked, and the opponent develops pieces while chasing it. You will see this again in the opening lessons.

steps.question: Retrieval check: the queen moves like which two pieces combined?
Retrieval check: about how many pawns is a queen worth?
steps.explain: Standard values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9.
